He then added, “I don’t want to talk about him too much, because I know a lot of clubs would love to have him in their squad, and he is very important to me. “He has that quality on the ball, covers a lot of ground, he is truly top class! I am really happy to have him, and he is going to play a key role in the team. “Keeping him? I am very hopeful he will stay. I think he is happy in Monaco. So if he stays, he can play a key role in my game plan.” Those quotes underline the challenge for Liverpool. Mid-season deals for highly rated midfielders are difficult at the best of times, and Monaco’s domestic situation could push them towards keeping one of their most valuable assets. At the same time, the source report notes that finances may influence the final decision if a sufficiently strong offer arrives. Our View Camara feels like the sort of move that makes a lot of sense. Liverpool do not need to force a January signing for the sake of it, but if a top young midfielder is attainable and the path has opened up because Chelsea have stepped back, that is exactly the kind of opportunity the club should be ready to take. The most encouraging part of this report is that Liverpool were not scrambling late, they were planning. Making contact on deadline day and effectively saying there could be a future move shows conviction. It also suggests Camara has already been sold on the project to some extent, or at least understands where he sits in Liverpool’s thinking. The quotes from Filipe Luis are huge praise, and they do raise expectations. Calling him “one of the best midfielders in the world” is not casual language. If Monaco are under pressure financially, Liverpool should test the waters with a serious offer and see where it leads. Iraola needs options, energy and control in the middle of the pitch. Camara sounds like a player who could give all three. If the conditions are right, this is one worth pushing hard for.

The journalist confirmed that his customary ‘here we go’ on the youngster’s transfer to Real Madrid is coming soon. Romano also addresses rumours that Real Madrid may not be signing him since Jose Mourinho has clearly stated he doesn’t want new players in January. Romano clarified that JJ Gabriel doesn’t necessarily qualify as a traditional winter reinforcement for Real Madrid. He is more of a long-term signing. This should come as a relief for Real Madrid fans, with the club now all set to get their hands on one of the most exciting prospects in England. What’s the update on the deal? JJ Gabriel will soon become a Real Madrid player. (Photo by Alex Livesey/Getty Images) As far as the deal is concerned, it is confirmed that JJ Gabriel will leave Manchester United, having already announced his exit on social media. Real Madrid, for their part, have also reportedly reached an agreement with the player. It was last reported that the deal only needs to be ratified by FIFA. Real Madrid, though, weren’t too happy with the fact that the leaks of the JJ Gabriel signing became public. JJ Gabriel, for his part, has remained silent on his future. His transfer is being handled by his representatives, who have already made big demands to all the interested parties, including a hefty salary package and a proper guarantee of a first-team ascension. At Real Madrid, Gabriel is likely to become a part of the RM Castilla setup, before eventually working his way up through the ranks.

title: Vitor Roque opens up on Barcelona struggles and lack of support: ‘They barely spoke to me’
summary: Former Barcelona forward Vitor Roque has reflected on his difficult spell at the Catalan club, admitting that he struggled with an injury, lacked the support he needed and was unable to meet expectati...
content: Vitor Roque opens up on Barcelona struggles and lack of support: ‘They barely spoke to me’ Former Barcelona forward Vitor Roque has reflected on his difficult spell at the Catalan club, admitting that he struggled with an injury, lacked the support he needed and was unable to meet expectations after arriving as a teenager. In an interview with AS , the Brazilian striker discussed his experience at Barcelona, the pressure placed on young South American players and the lessons he learned from a challenging period in European football. Roque, now at Palmeiras, also expressed gratitude to former teammates who helped him during his time in Spain. The 21-year-old joined Barcelona from Athletico Paranaense in January 2024, but his time at the club proved short-lived. After making 16 appearances and scoring twice, he moved to Real Betis on loan before returning to Brazil in February 2025. Vitor Roque reveals injury problems behind Barcelona struggles Roque explained that his Barcelona move came while he was still recovering from a syndesmotic injury, which had required surgery before his departure from Brazil. “I went to Barcelona when I was 18. It was a dream come true: playing for one of the biggest clubs in the world. It was a bit difficult. It was a bit difficult. “I went there with a syndesmotic injury, which I should have had surgery for at Athletico Paranaense but didn’t. I arrived in a lot of pain – quite a lot, actually. “During that time, I was doing physiotherapy, trying to get into the best possible shape, but in the end we didn’t manage it. “I wasn’t able to perform at the highest level in football and I think that was part of the process. Vitor Roque spent a short loan tenure at Real Betis. (Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images) “I know that God has everything planned out, yes. It didn’t work out there; it wasn’t what I’d expected. Afterwards, I went to Betis and I couldn’t perform there either. “But today at Palmeiras I feel good; I feel at home. People have helped me a lot and, thank God, I’m happy,” he explained. Roque explains lack of patience with young players Roque believes young players are often expected to perform immediately after making major transfers, despite the challenges of adapting to a new country, language and environment. There have been cases in La Liga itself, like Franco Mastantuono and Endrick, where young South Americans moved a bit too early to Europe, but have failed to earn regular football. “People think that when we young players arrive, we have to start playing at 100 per cent straight away, giving it our all and playing our best football, but that’s not how it works. It takes patience. “Sometimes we don’t have the time we need to settle in. We’re very young, and speaking a new language is really difficult. Sometimes it’s important to have the manager’s support, and when I went to Barcelona, I didn’t have that. “They barely spoke to me, you know? So I think you have to bear that in mind, and a lot of people don’t see it that way – they think you have to be ready from the very first minute.” The Brazilian also explained what he learned from the experience, stating, “I learnt that whatever happens, you have to work hard, give it your all and make the most of the opportunities you’re given, however small they may sometimes be. Vitor Roque spent a forgettable tenure at Barcelona. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images) “You have to be there, giving it your all, because nobody’s going to do what only you can do for yourself. So you have to keep working with a lot of humility so that things eventually fall into place on their own.” Roque admits regret but is happy at Palmeiras Although Roque acknowledged that he still feels some regret about how his Barcelona career unfolded, he believes it is important to move forward. “Well, obviously I still feel a bit of regret, so to speak, but I think in football you shouldn’t dwell on that. “It’s something I’ve already come to terms with, and now I’m happy here at Palmeiras. That’s the most important thing. Now it’s time to write a new chapter.” Roque also singled out Raphinha and Ronald Araujo as important figures during his Barcelona spell, while mentioning Natan among the friends he made at Real Betis. “I used to hang out a lot with Raphinha, who helped me enormously. He’s an incredible bloke and gave me a huge helping hand throughout the whole process. “Ronald Araújo, who’s now at Liverpool, was another person who also helped me a lot, and I’m very fond of him. I left several friends behind at Betis, such as Natan, who helped me a lot too.” Lastly, he revealed that he is in contact with Barcelona’s younger generation and continues to follow their progress. “Yes, of course. They’re teammates I’ve played with and they’ve been brilliant to me. I still follow all their successes closely and I’m really happy for them,” he concluded.

title: Written in the stars! Juan Sebastian Veron eyes Copa Libertadores glory as Estudiantes face Palmeiras at scene of father's 1968 triumph
summary: Estudiantes president Juan Sebastian Veron has expressed confidence ahead of Saturday's Copa Libertadores final against Palmeiras at Montevideo's Estadio Centenario. Returning to the exact stadium and opponent where his father Juan Ramon inspired the club's first continental title in 1968, Veron backed a new generation to seize the moment.
content: Estudiantes v Boca Juniors - Copa de la Liga Profesional 2024 - Getty Images Sport Estudiantes president Juan Sebastian Veron has expressed confidence ahead of Saturday's Copa Libertadores final against Palmeiras at Montevideo's Estadio Centenario. Returning to the exact stadium and opponent where his father Juan Ramon inspired the club's first continental title in 1968, Veron backed a new generation to seize the moment. Veron backs Estudiantes ahead of Palmeiras showdown According to ESPN , Estudiantes president Juan Sebastian Veron has voiced full belief in his squad upon arriving in Uruguay for Saturday's CONMEBOL Libertadores final against Palmeiras at the Estadio Centenario. Having eliminated Flamengo on penalties at the Maracana to reach the showpiece, the Argentine side stand one win away from a fifth continental crown. "The expectation is to play a great match, and we're sure we will, because the team has been playing well," Veron said. "We don't need to say much to the players, because they are aware of their position and how hard they fought to be here. It's clear the fans are behind them. From our side, we only have words of gratitude." 'These places are for the few, and we are one of them' The former Inter and Lazio playmaker emphasised the importance of guiding a younger generation of Estudiantes players through the pressure of a continental decider while drawing strength from local support in Montevideo. "I think it's part of the process, experiencing these moments. Beyond the nerves and everything that's at stake, knowing that these places are for the few, and we are one of them," he noted. "Luckily, it's happened to us quite a bit in our history. This time it's happening again, and other generations are experiencing it. Despite the differences, Argentinians and Uruguayans have a very similar way of seeing football, and you can feel it." A remarkable Veron family circle from 1968 to 2026 The fixture carries extraordinary historical weight for the Veron family, reuniting Estudiantes with the exact opponent and venue of their maiden Libertadores triumph in 1968. Back then, Juan Sebastian's father, Juan Ramon 'La Bruja' Veron, scored in all three final matches—including the decisive 2-0 victory at the Estadio Centenario—before inspiring a three-peat in 1969 and 1970. The former Manchester United and Chelsea midfielder later captained Estudiantes to their fourth Libertadores title against Cruzeiro in 2009 after returning from Europe, though he always kept his father's legacy in perspective. "At Estudiantes I won three titles, but my dad won five... in almost all of them he was a key player or the absolute protagonist," he once reflected, also recalling: "I never felt any kind of pressure other than the internal kind." From captain on the pitch to president in the stands Having first taken over the club presidency in 2014, Veron now experiences the final from the directors' box rather than wearing the captain's armband in midfield. "As a player, I have good memories at the Centenario. I hope to have similar satisfaction as a club official," Veron concluded ahead of Saturday's kick-off in Montevideo.

title: Lucas Herbert Reveals He Is Still Owed ‘A Lot’ of Money by LIV Golf
summary: Lucas Herbert has revealed he is still owed a lot of money by LIV Golf following the league's collapse. The Australian said he has accepted that he may not recover much of what he is owed after dealing with legal issues during his time with the league. Herbert spoke to Fox Sports Australia about his …
content: | Source: Lastwordonsports.com - Ajayi Segun Lucas Herbert has revealed he is still owed a lot of money by LIV Golf following the league’s collapse. The Australian said he has accepted that he may not recover much of what he is owed after dealing with legal issues during his time with the league. Herbert spoke to Fox Sports Australia about his experience with LIV Golf, admitting that the process of recovering unpaid money could take a long time. He also said he had moved on and was no longer expecting much from the situation. The former LIV Golf player also opened up about the league’s poor communication with players, which he said contributed to the lack of interest in the proposed LIV Golf 2.0. ALSO READ: Jackson Koivun Doubles Career Earnings After Dramatic Win Over Brooks Koepka Lucas Herbert Does Not Expect to Recover Much of His Money Herbert admitted that he is unlikely to receive much of the money LIV Golf still owes him. The 30-year-old said he has accepted the situation and is not expecting the legal process to bring much back. However, LIV Golf’s bankruptcy filings listed Herbert as being owed just over $1 million. The Australian was among the league’s unsecured creditors, with $1,012,204.95 still outstanding under his player participation agreement. “You’re probably foolish to think you’re going to get much of it (owed money). Anything from this point is going to be a bonus,” he said. “It’s a long drawn out process with mostly lawyers winning out of the whole battle. I’ve accepted that and moved on. The reality is I made a lot of money at the same time as I’m owed a lot.” Herbert also revealed that legal issues during his time with LIV Golf took a lot of energy out of him. Although he enjoyed playing on the league, he said those problems affected his experience. “As great as a time I had on the LIV tour, I had many legal issues along the way, which drew a lot of energy out of me. I’ve played this game a few times now and I’m going to expect not very much and hopefully be pleasantly surprised, rather than the other way around.” ALSO READ: Bryson DeChambeau’s Agency Lands Major Investment From Former LIV Golf Bidder Lucas Herbert Criticises LIV Golf’s Communication With Players Herbert also spoke about how players were kept informed during LIV Golf’s final season. He said players often found out about important developments through media reports rather than directly from the league. “I’ve got no problem saying we were poorly communicated with as players throughout the season. A lot of times mainstream media, or media outlets outside of LIV, knew more about what was going on than we did, which was pretty tough to deal with. It was a bit of a contributing factor as to why very few guys were interested in going around again in 2.0.” The Australian said the lack of communication played a part in players losing interest in the league’s proposed relaunch. LIV Golf’s plans for 2.0 failed to move forward after it struggled to get enough players to commit. Herbert’s comments add to the fallout following LIV Golf’s collapse, with players and businesses still waiting to see how much of the money owed to them will be recovered. title: Tomas Berdych issues strong criticism of key Davis Cup rule after losing to Italy, ‘I’m not a fan of it’
summary: The Davis Cup is a tournament that boasts a long and rich history, and over the years has gained importance among players. After all, whilst...
content: The Davis Cup is a tournament that boasts a long and rich history, and over the years has gained importance among players. After all, whilst the Grand Slams almost always take priority, the opportunity to represent one’s country in a team format, which is totally unique for such a solo sport, intrigued many. Despite all they have achieved, the likes of Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic count memories of this tournament up amongst their very best, highlighting the importance of the Davis Cup . However, there’s no denying that it feels like, of late, it has lost its sparkle. There are many possible explanations for the waning interest in what should be a thrilling spectacle, dubbed ‘the World Cup of Tennis’. Tomas Berdych has outlined one of the outstanding problems in his post-match press conference following yesterday’s loss to Italy in the semi-finals. Tomas Berdych criticises the Davis Cup final being played in one country It had been a fine campaign for the Czechia team, spearheaded by stars like Jakub Mensik, Jiri Lehecka and Tomas Machac. However, they can feel mightily unlucky to be heading home, having only lost to the three-time defending champions Italy in their back garden on the deciding tiebreak of the deciding rubber. Asked afterwards how much of a disadvantage playing in front of an Italian crowd was during the match, Berdych used this opportunity to express his wider frustration with the new format. He complained: “I’m not a fan of it. This is one of the reasons. It’s been decided that it’s going to happen in one country; that country will always be in the final, that’s it. Photo by Emmanuele Ciancaglini/Getty Images for World Tennis “That’s not what Davis Cup is. It’s just some of the decisions that someone’s made. That’s how I see it. It’s a competition that used to be played for more than a hundred years in some kind of a format. It just completely changed. That’s how it is.” Berdych was keen not to look like a sore loser, and so recalled his side’s win in Serbia, and how good that felt. However, his point is a hugely valid one, and he concluded: “It’s not a complaint that you play in a country against the crowd. It’s just the overall… “The fans were amazingly fair. It was so nice to play in such an atmosphere. I mean, I can compare you to the ones that we were kind of scared. When you play in Argentina, it was completely different level. “It’s still something that I would choose more than this.” Why did the Davis Cup change its format? The format of the Davis Cup splits qualifying for the grand finale into a series of ties played across the year. By the 2010s, knockout matches featured in February, July, September and November, with the key selling point being the best-of-five-set home and away ties in venues around the globe. However, regular complaints about the calendar eventually forced change, with the Davis Cup deemed flexible enough to facilitate. The fact that so many top players often skipped the tournament further justified such bold alterations. However, the overhaul has not gone down well, and across 2018 and 2019, Barcelona football legend Gerard Pique conjured a deal between the ITF and his company Kosmos, replacing later rounds with an 18-team, week-long event in November at one venue. This partnership was scrapped in 2023, and nowadays home and away ties are played during qualifying, but just one city hosts the ‘Final 8’, where the eight best teams enter a knockout tournament held within a week.

title: Australian wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38, WWE says
summary: Tributes have flooded in for the 38-year-old Australian who is survived by his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter.
content: [WWE via Getty Images] Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced. The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details. Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague." They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter. WWE has been contacted for further comment. Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday. The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd. Owens said Haley loved performing. "I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said. "Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed." WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!" WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother." WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005. Bronson Reed in action against Dragon Lee during RAW in New York in November. [WWE via Getty Images] Australian pro wrestler Brendan Vink, who goes by Duke Hanson, posted "I love you, Jermaine." on X. According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during the WWE Crown Jewel event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia earlier in November. He did not have a match during the event but was tossed off the stage and through a set of tables during a brawl. Haley initially competed around the independent wrestling scene as Jonah Rock and J-Rock before signing with WWE in 2019. He was released in 2021 before returning a year and continuing with WWE up until his death. In 2024, he won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal. Haley is the second wrestler to die in the last few months after Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star passed away at the age of 40 in September. No cause of death was provided at the time.
